title: Dignity, privacy, comfort, rest and sleep
blurb: Deliver the fundamentals of care with dignity and privacy, and protect comfort, rest and sleep in hospital.
question: Mrs Begum, 84, has slept badly for three nights on a busy medical ward. Her NEWS2 has been 0 throughout, but she is woken at 02:00 and 06:00 for observations and dozes most of the afternoon. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Dignity means treating each person as a valued individual, with respect for their privacy, choices, culture and body. The NMC Code (clause 1) asks you to treat people with kindness, respect and compassion, avoid assumptions, recognise diversity and individual choice, and deliver the fundamentals of care effectively and without undue delay. In plain English: the small things (a closed curtain, a knock, a choice of clothes, a call bell answered promptly) are the care.

teach.h: The Code on dignity and the fundamentals
head: Clause
What you must do
rows: Treat people with kindness, respect and compassion
Deliver the fundamentals of care effectively
Avoid assumptions; recognise diversity and choice
Respect and uphold people's human rights
Respect privacy in all aspects of care
teach.caption: The fundamentals of care include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and keeping people in clean and hygienic conditions (Code, clause 1 note).

items: Close curtains or doors fully (use dignity clips) and tell the person before you start.
Expose only the part of the body you need; cover the rest.
Ask how the person likes to be addressed, and use that name.
Ask about and record cultural, religious and gender preferences for personal care, then plan to meet them.
Speak to the person directly, in plain words, even when others are present.
Answer call bells promptly and leave the bell and drinks within reach.

teach.h: Rest and sleep are part of recovery
teach.body: Poor sleep worsens pain, mood and confusion, and sleep disturbance can be an early sign of delirium. NICE CG103 asks staff to promote good sleep by avoiding nursing or medical procedures during sleeping hours if possible, scheduling medication rounds so they do not disturb sleep, and reducing noise at night. The registered nurse can review observation timing when NEWS2 allows (a score of 0 needs a minimum of 12-hourly observations).

rows.label: Drinks
values: Tea, coffee or alcohol late on

teach.caption: NHS insomnia advice (reviewed 2024): avoid caffeine, alcohol and smoking for at least 6 hours before bed. Sleeping pills are usually only for a few days or weeks at most.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Begum on the medical ward
teach.body: Mrs Begum's NEWS2 is 0, so the minimum observation frequency is 12-hourly. The nurse discusses with the team moving her observations out of the night, groups any night-time care into one visit, and offers an eye mask and earplugs. During the day she encourages Mrs Begum to sit out, walk with support and limit long naps. She checks for pain, a full bladder or worry keeping her awake, and documents the plan so the night team follows it.

teach.caption: A person who rings repeatedly at night is often uncomfortable, cold, in pain or needing the toilet: meet the need and plan regular checks.

steps.label: Prepare
steps.sub: Explain, privacy, linen ready, bed at working height

steps.label: Two staff
steps.sub: One each side; check any lines, drains, catheter

steps.label: Roll and tuck
steps.sub: Roll to one side, change half, roll back

steps.label: Safety
steps.sub: Bed low, brakes on, call bell in reach

teach.caption: For an unconscious person, one nurse also protects the airway and head during each roll.

teach.text: Do not reach for a hypnotic first. Insomnia in hospital usually has a cause (noise, light, pain, a full bladder, anxiety, daytime napping, night-time observations). Fix the cause and the routine first; sleeping tablets are short-term only and add falls and confusion risk.

items: Code 1: kindness, no assumptions, fundamentals of care without undue delay; Code 5.1: privacy in all aspects of care.
Fundamentals include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling, hygiene.
Ask about and record cultural, religious and gender preferences; plan care to meet them.
Protect sleep: avoid night procedures, time medicines and observations sensibly, reduce noise (CG103).
Sleep hygiene before sleeping pills; pills are for days to weeks at most.

summary: You can now apply the Code's duties on dignity, privacy and the fundamentals of care to everyday nursing, including personal preferences and bed making. You can also protect rest and sleep on a ward using NICE CG103 and sleep hygiene before medication.

A.q: Mr Evans, 80, is in a four-bed bay and needs help on to a commode. The curtains do not fully close and his neighbour has a visitor. What should the nurse do?
options: Help him quickly, as the curtains are mostly closed
Ask the visitor to leave the bay until he is finished
Close the gap with a dignity clip and tell him first
Wait until visiting time ends before helping him
A.why: Code 5.1: respect privacy in all aspects of care. Closing the gap fully and explaining first protects privacy without delaying care (Code 1.4).

whyNot.0: A partly open curtain still exposes him; speed does not replace privacy.
whyNot.1: Removing the neighbour's visitor is unnecessary if the curtain is properly closed.
whyNot.3: Making him wait for the toilet is undue delay in a fundamental of care (Code 1.4).

A.q: Mr Sharma, 70, a Sikh man, asks during admission that his hair is not cut and that he keeps his kara (steel bangle) on. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Explain that hospital policy requires jewellery to be removed
Record his wishes and plan care around them
Agree verbally but leave it out of the records for privacy
Ask his family whether these wishes really need to be met
A.why: Code 1.3: recognise diversity and individual choice. Documenting religious preferences in the care plan lets every shift respect them; any clinical conflict is discussed with him.

whyNot.0: A blanket rule ignores individual choice; any genuine clinical need would be discussed and agreed with him.
whyNot.2: If it is not recorded, the next shift may not know and may breach his wishes.
whyNot.3: He has capacity and has stated his wishes; asking family to second-guess them is disrespectful.

A.q: Which of the following does the NMC Code list among the fundamentals of care?
options: Medicines reconciliation
Discharge planning
Bladder and bowel care
Wound swabbing
A.why: The Code states the fundamentals of care include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and keeping people clean and hygienic.

whyNot.0: Medicines reconciliation matters but is not named in the Code's fundamentals list.
whyNot.1: Discharge planning is important but is not one of the named fundamentals.
whyNot.3: Wound swabbing is a clinical procedure, not one of the named fundamentals.

B.q: Mr Reid, 73, says he cannot sleep on the ward because of noise and the lights at the nurses' station. He has no pain. Which intervention should be tried first?
options: Ask the doctor to prescribe a short course of a hypnotic
Reduce noise and light and offer an eye mask
Move him to a side room set aside for infection control
Give him a cup of tea to help him relax before settling
B.why: NICE CG103 rec 1.4.13: reduce noise to a minimum during sleep periods. Simple environmental measures come before medication.

whyNot.0: Hypnotics are a later option and carry falls and confusion risk.
whyNot.2: Isolation rooms are allocated by infection risk, not for sleep.
whyNot.3: Tea contains caffeine, which hinders sleep; NHS advice is to avoid it before bed.

B.q: Doris, 76, is unconscious after a stroke and needs her bottom sheet changed. Two staff are available. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Lift her clear of the bed while the second person changes it
Slide her to the top of the bed and change the lower half
Leave the sheet until she is next sat out of bed
Roll her to each side in turn, changing half each time
B.why: Rolling an occupied bed, one nurse each side, avoids manual lifting (Manual Handling Operations Regulations: avoid, assess, reduce) while protecting her airway and skin.

whyNot.0: Manually lifting a person is hazardous handling that should be avoided.
whyNot.1: Dragging her up the bed causes shear and risks skin damage.
whyNot.2: Leaving soiled or creased linen risks skin damage and breaches the fundamentals of care.

B.q: Miss Clarke, 88, rings her call bell repeatedly at night. When the nurse answers, she says she is cold, uncomfortable and needs the toilet. Her pain score is 1/10. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Toilet her, warm and reposition her and plan regular checks
Move the call bell further away so that she rests without ringing
Ask the doctor to prescribe night sedation to help her settle
Explain that staff are busy and she should ring in emergencies
B.why: Repeated calls usually signal unmet needs. Meeting her comfort and toileting needs and planning checks delivers the fundamentals of care (Code 1.2, 1.4).

whyNot.1: Removing the call bell is unsafe and neglects her needs.
whyNot.2: Sedation does not meet the needs she has described and raises falls risk.
whyNot.3: Discouraging calls breaches the Code's duty of kindness and timely care.

C.q: Mrs Begum, 84, has a NEWS2 of 0 and has had observations at 02:00 and 06:00 for three nights. She is sleeping poorly and dozing in the afternoons. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue the current observations because older patients may deteriorate
Ask for a hypnotic so that she sleeps through the night-time checks
Review her observation timing with the team to protect her night sleep
Encourage her to nap for longer in the afternoon to catch up on rest
C.why: NEWS2 Chart 4: a score of 0 needs a minimum of 12-hourly observations, so night checks can often be rescheduled. CG103 advises avoiding procedures during sleeping hours.

whyNot.0: Frequency should match NEWS2 and clinical judgement; routine night checks are not needed at a score of 0.
whyNot.1: Medication should not be used to accommodate unnecessary night-time care.
whyNot.3: Long daytime naps worsen night-time sleep, according to NHS sleep advice.

C.q: Olivia, 23, has a learning disability and is anxious on admission. On the ward round, several staff discuss her care at the bedside using medical terms and talk to her mother rather than to her. What should the nurse do?
options: Let the discussion continue as her mother knows her best
Speak to Olivia directly in plain language and include her
Explain the plan to Olivia later once the round has finished
Ask her mother to sign the care plan on Olivia's behalf
C.why: Code 1.3 and 7.1: avoid assumptions and use terms people understand. Olivia should be involved directly, with reasonable adjustments, and her mother involved as she wishes.

whyNot.0: Assuming her mother should speak for her ignores Olivia's right to be involved.
whyNot.2: Explaining afterwards still excludes her from decisions being made about her.
whyNot.3: A parent cannot sign for an adult; capacity is presumed unless shown otherwise (MCA s1).

C.q: Mr Novak, 79, has been prescribed a hypnotic for poor sleep on the ward. On assessment he naps most afternoons, drinks coffee in the evening and is woken by a noisy bay. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Give the hypnotic each night and review it at discharge
Move his hypnotic earlier so that it works before bay noise
Swap evening coffee for tea and keep the hypnotic as it is
Address naps, caffeine and noise and review the hypnotic
C.why: NHS insomnia advice: deal with causes and sleep habits first; sleeping pills are only for a few days or weeks at most. Hypnotics also increase falls risk in older people, so review the prescription.

whyNot.0: Continuing until discharge without addressing the causes risks dependence and falls.
whyNot.1: Retiming the dose does not deal with naps, caffeine or noise.
whyNot.2: Tea also contains caffeine, and the hypnotic still needs review.

reteach.title: See the ward through the patient's eyes
reteach.question: Imagine lying in bed 4 for a night. What would make you feel exposed, ignored or unable to sleep?

blocks.body: A curtain left open, a conversation over your head, a light on all night or a call bell out of reach all tell a patient they matter less. Turning those around is how the Code's duties of kindness, privacy and timely fundamentals of care become real. The same lens explains poor sleep: noise, light, pain, a full bladder and checks at 02:00 are the usual culprits.

blocks.h: A memory aid: CLOSE the curtain on poor dignity

blocks.text: Speed is not a substitute for privacy, and sedation is not a substitute for a calm, dark, quiet night.

explain.body: Code 1: kindness, respect, no assumptions, fundamentals of care without undue delay, human rights. Code 5.1: privacy in all aspects of care. Fundamentals include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and hygiene.

test.q: Which Code clause requires care to be delivered without undue delay?
test.why: Code 1.4: make sure any treatment, assistance or care is delivered without undue delay.

whyNot.0: 1.2 is delivering the fundamentals of care effectively.
whyNot.2: 5.1 is respecting privacy in all aspects of care.
whyNot.3: 1.3 is avoiding assumptions and recognising diversity.

explain.body: Ask about cultural, religious and gender preferences for personal care, record them in the care plan and plan care to meet them. Close curtains fully, expose only what is needed and speak to the person directly.

test.q: Mr Ali asks for a male nurse for intimate care. What should happen?
options: Record it and arrange care to meet it
Tell him staffing makes this impossible
Agree but keep it out of the records
Ask him to justify the request first
test.why: Code 1.3: recognise individual choice. Recording the preference means every shift can plan for it.

whyNot.1: Refusing without trying ignores his preference; if it cannot be met, discuss options with him.
whyNot.2: Unrecorded preferences are easily missed by the next shift.
whyNot.3: He does not need to justify a reasonable personal preference.

explain.body: CG103 1.4.13: avoid procedures during sleeping hours where possible, schedule medicine rounds to avoid waking people, reduce noise. NEWS2 0 needs observations at least 12-hourly, so night checks can often move.

test.q: What is the minimum observation frequency for a NEWS2 score of 0?
options: Every hour
4-hourly
6-hourly
12-hourly
test.why: NEWS2 Chart 4: a score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

whyNot.0: Hourly is the minimum for a score of 5 or more, or 3 in one parameter.
whyNot.1: 4–6 hourly is the minimum for a total of 1–4.
whyNot.2: 6-hourly is the upper end of the 1–4 band, not the 0 band.

explain.body: Regular routine, short or no daytime naps, no caffeine, alcohol or smoking for 6 hours before bed, a dark quiet room. Sleeping pills are usually only for a few days or weeks at most; insomnia lasting 3 months or more is long-term.

test.q: According to NHS advice, insomnia lasting how long is called long-term insomnia?
options: 2 weeks or longer
1 month or longer
3 months or longer
6 months or longer
test.why: NHS insomnia advice: insomnia lasting 3 months or longer is called long-term insomnia.

whyNot.1: 1 month is still short of the 3-month threshold.
whyNot.3: 6 months is longer than the stated threshold.
